newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia orders slaughter of snowed-in livestock.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia orders slaughter of snowed-in livestock.

text.p: Mongolia has ordered local authorities to slaughter weak livestock to save precious supplies of fodder for more than four million cattle threatened by heavy autumn snows, a senior minister said on Thursday.
Snow banks up to one metre (three ft) deep had buried grasslands in 73 counties, making it difficult for herders to feed at least 4.6 million head of cattle, Defence Minister D. Dorligjav said.
"The base of the country's economy -- cattle -- is threatened," Dorligjav told Reuters in an interview.
"We are facing the question of whether we can keep the cattle alive in snowy areas by transporting fodder there, or whether we must slaughter them."

Local governments had been ordered to kill the weakest animals in nomadic herds of cattle, sheep and goats, because it was obvious the herds could not be sustained with state supplies of fodder, he said.
It was not yet possible to estimate how many animals would have to be slaughtered, he added.

Mongolia's hardy livestock usually survive the harsh winters that sweep across this huge but sparsely populated north Asian nation by eating dried grass on the vast steppes, which are normally only covered by a thin layer of snow.
In recent weeks, heavy snowfalls have blanketed vast areas of grassland, burying the precious grass and making it almost impossible to move cattle to better pastures.

Dorligjav said the cash-strapped government was no longer able to fly fodder and aid to the affected areas because of fuel shortages, but was sending special equipment to try to reopen sections of the crude road network.
Mongolia had yet to decide whether to buy foreign fodder to make up for the grass shortfall, he said.
Ample food stocks were helping thousands of nomads survive the deep snows better than their livestock, he added, although at least one person had frozen to death on a blocked road.
The heavy snows are the latest blow to Mongolia's fragile economy, which has struggled from crisis to crisis since the collapse of its former sponsor the Soviet Union.
On Wednesday, Ulan Bator received $945,000 in aid from the United States, including blankets, winter clothes and food, the official Ardiin Erkh newspaper said on Thursday.
